analysis.one_liner: Phases out the capital gains tax entirely and exempts estates up to $1 million.
analysis.headline: The House never voted on this bill, which would have cut the individual capital gains tax rate from 14% down to 0% by 2011 and exempted estates up to $1 million from estate tax.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have gradually eliminated the federal capital gains tax for individuals — lowering the rate from 14% in 1997 to 0% by 2011 — while cutting the corporate capital gains rate from 28% to 14% over the same period [S2][S3]. It would also have roughly doubled the estate tax exemption, from $600,000 to $1 million, and raised the special valuation break for inherited farms from $750,000 to $1 million [S3]. It was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and never received a vote before Congress ended [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: The biggest winners would be households and corporations that realize large capital gains, since capital gains income is concentrated among the wealthiest Americans — the rate falling to 0% by 2011 would eliminate their tax on investment profits entirely [S2][S3]. Estates above the then-current $600,000 exemption — especially owners of family farms and closely held small businesses — would gain from the higher $1 million unified credit and the larger farm valuation break [S3]. The 3 Republican cosponsors and tax-cut advocates would also gain a legislative talking point.

how_it_helps.text: Individuals: the bill replaces the existing capital gains rate with a declining schedule — 14% of net capital gain taxed in 1997, dropping one point a year to 0% in 2011 and after — and applies the same declining rate under the alternative minimum tax.
Corporations: the alternative tax on net capital gains starts at 28% in 1997 and steps down to 14% by 2011 and after.
Estates: the unified estate and gift tax credit would rise to cover the tax on $1 million (up from $600,000), and the filing threshold in section 6018(a) would rise from $600,000 to $1,000,000.

Family farms and certain other real property: the maximum valuation reduction under the special-use rules of section 2032A would rise from $750,000 to $1,000,000, letting heirs value inherited farm land at its farm-use value rather than market value.

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury. The bill contains no offsetting revenue provisions, so the revenue lost from phasing capital gains tax to zero, cutting the corporate rate, and raising the estate exemption would have to be made up through other taxes, lower federal spending, or more borrowing. Because capital gains and large taxable estates are concentrated among the wealthiest households, the missing revenue is a cost spread across general taxpayers in exchange for tax cuts concentrated at the top.
analysis.who_pays_short: General taxpayers through lost federal revenue

drawbacks.text: The tax cuts are concentrated where the assets are: households that own stocks, businesses, and appreciated property — predominantly the wealthiest — would capture most of the benefit, while the bill gives wage earners with little in capital gains or no taxable estate little direct relief.

The bill is not paid for: it has no revenue offsets, so a permanent phaseout of the capital gains tax to 0% would steadily shrink federal revenue and force other taxes to rise, spending to fall, or deficits to grow.
Raising the estate exemption to $1 million primarily benefits estates large enough to owe estate tax under the $600,000 threshold then in law; most families would see no change.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The estate tax relief for family farms and small business owners is a genuine, targeted benefit, and lower capital gains rates do modestly help small savers. But the bill's dominant provisions — a capital gains rate falling to zero for individuals and down to 14% for corporations — are an unstructured, permanent tax cut whose benefits flow overwhelmingly to holders of large accumulated wealth, with nothing in the bill to replace the lost revenue. The farm and small business relief could have been delivered at a fraction of the cost.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and sat there for the rest of the Congress; the House never voted on it.

narrative.text: Rep. Michael Pappas introduced the bill on January 7, 1997, the opening day of the 105th Congress, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day.
On March 6, 1997, Pappas delivered introductory remarks on the bill — the only activity beyond the referral.
No further action was ever taken: the Ways and Means Committee never marked it up and the House never voted on it before the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died in committee without a vote, holders of large capital gains and large estates gained nothing beyond the tax rules already in place, and general taxpayers were spared an unfunded tax cut weighted toward the wealthiest households. Its sponsors gained only the record of having introduced it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Taxpayers generally; the bill simply died

for.name: Rep. Michael Pappas
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on January 7, 1997 and delivered introductory remarks on March 6, 1997.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never took the bill up after its January 7, 1997 referral; no markup, no vote, no report for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 3 cosponsors were Republicans, and no votes were ever taken to test broader support in either party.

industries.note: A capital gains rate falling to 0% by 2011 would eliminate tax on investment profits entirely for the households that realize most capital gains — the wealthiest — while the lost revenue falls on general taxpayers through other taxes, cuts, or debt.
The bill cuts the corporate alternative tax on capital gains from 28% to 14% over fifteen years, letting corporations that sell appreciated assets keep more of the proceeds.

industries.industry: Family farms and closely held small businesses
industries.note: Heirs of farm owners would benefit from the higher $1 million unified credit and the larger $1 million special-use valuation cap, making it easier to keep inherited farms and businesses in the family rather than sell to pay estate tax.
